framing: The best allocation depends on the objective
paragraphs: Choosing a model size also commits the team to a data appetite and a future serving bill. A compact model trained for longer might be expensive to create yet cheaper to use. A larger model might reach a loss target with less training work and still exceed the available serving memory. Parameter count alone cannot settle either decision.

Scaling laws make the tradeoffs explicit by fitting how loss changes with model size, tokens, and compute. Their apparent simplicity is useful and dangerous. A familiar ratio can hide a different counting convention, optimizer, or data distribution. A fitted loss forecast also answers a narrower question than whether a model follows instructions, writes correct code, or meets a product's reliability requirement.

This chapter derives the dominant matrix-multiplication estimate for training work, compares Kaplan and Chinchilla allocations, and follows the consequences of including lifetime inference demand. You will calculate a break-even volume and fit a two-term loss surface, then see how finite dataset size and a missed intermediate checkpoint change the proposed run. Worked numerical examples keep the arithmetic inspectable, while real launch decisions still rest on held-out task evaluations and measured runs.

The preceding chapters covered dataset provenance, filtering, and how supervision earns trust. Now you can ask how far an available data pool and a compute budget can take a training run. Gradients, elementary calculus, and logarithms help with the derivations. Keep the held-out evaluations from earlier chapters available, since low next-token loss cannot replace them. The next chapter turns a token target into a data pipeline, where filtering, repetition, and packing determine what the model actually receives.
outcomes: Derive a parameter-and-token allocation under stated assumptions.
Calculate when lower serving work offsets additional training work.
Identify extrapolations that require new measurements before a large run.
question: Which evidence would make you change an attractive allocation before spending the full training budget?
